prompt: What is the core claim of Kant's 'Copernican revolution' in philosophy?
options: Knowledge must conform to mind-independent objects
Objects of experience must conform to the structures of the knowing mind
All knowledge is empirical and derives from the senses
Reality is reducible to mathematical equations
correctAnswer: Objects of experience must conform to the structures of the knowing mind
explanation: Kant inverted the traditional picture: instead of the mind passively mirroring objects, objects of possible experience must conform to the a priori forms (space, time, the categories) that the mind brings to experience. He named this analogy after Copernicus: just as Copernicus moved the observer rather than the heavens, Kant moved the structure to the knower.

prompt: In Kant's system, the 'thing-in-itself' (noumenon) is:
options: The fully knowable inner essence of an object
Reality as it exists independently of any mind, knowable only through pure reason
A limiting concept marking what lies beyond possible experience
Identical to the phenomenon viewed from God's perspective
correctAnswer: A limiting concept marking what lies beyond possible experience
explanation: For Kant we can only know phenomena — appearances structured by our cognitive forms. The noumenon serves as a limiting concept: we must posit it (something must appear), but we cannot have positive theoretical knowledge of it. Reason that strains to know noumena generates the antinomies of pure reason.

prompt: Which of the following is, for Kant, a synthetic a priori judgement?
options: 'All bachelors are unmarried'
'It is raining'
'Some swans are black'
explanation: Synthetic a priori judgements add information yet are known independently of experience. Mathematical truths are Kant's paradigm. 'All bachelors are unmarried' is analytic (true by definition); 'it is raining' and 'some swans are black' are synthetic but a posteriori. Kant argues that without synthetic a priori judgements, mathematics and natural science would be unintelligible.

prompt: Hume argued causation was nothing but constant conjunction and habit. Kant's response was that:
options: Hume was right and metaphysics is impossible
Causation is a category the mind imposes as a condition of any coherent experience
Causation can be proved a posteriori from sufficient observation
Causation is a property of noumena directly accessible to reason
correctAnswer: Causation is a category the mind imposes as a condition of any coherent experience
explanation: Kant accepts Hume's point that we cannot derive necessary causal connection from experience alone, then turns it around: we must already presuppose causation in order to have any unified, intelligible experience at all. Causality is therefore a category of the understanding, not an empirical generalisation.

prompt: For Kant, space and time are:
options: Independently existing containers (Newton)
Relations between things-in-themselves (Leibniz)
Pure forms of human intuition
Empirical concepts built from sense impressions
correctAnswer: Pure forms of human intuition
explanation: Kant calls space and time the pure forms of outer and inner intuition: the necessary structures within which any sensible content must be received. They are not properties of noumena nor independent containers; they are conditions of possibility for human experience.

prompt: According to Kant, what is the only thing 'good without qualification'?
options: Happiness
A good will
Pleasure
Health
correctAnswer: A good will
explanation: Kant opens the Groundwork by arguing that talents, wealth, and even happiness can be misused by an evil agent. Only the good will — the will that acts from duty out of respect for the moral law — is unconditionally good. Its worth does not depend on consequences.

prompt: The Universal Law formulation of the Categorical Imperative says we should:
options: Act so as to maximise overall happiness
Act on maxims that we could will to become universal laws
Follow the customs of our community
Treat every act as if it were observed by God
correctAnswer: Act on maxims that we could will to become universal laws
explanation: Kant's first formulation: 'Act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' Lying promises fail the test because a world of universal lying would self-destruct: nobody would trust promises, so the maxim could not be willed universally without contradiction.

prompt: Kant's Humanity formulation of the Categorical Imperative forbids:
options: Any use of another person to achieve one's ends
Treating any rational being merely as a means and never also as an end
All forms of self-interest
Acting from personal inclination rather than duty
correctAnswer: Treating any rational being merely as a means and never also as an end
explanation: Kant's wording is precise: never treat humanity 'merely as a means'. Hiring a plumber uses them as a means, but consensually and respecting their dignity — that is fine. Slavery, deception, and coercion treat persons as if they had only instrumental value, ignoring their autonomy as rational ends.

prompt: For Kant, autonomy means:
options: Doing whatever one feels like
Acting on inclinations without external interference
Giving oneself the moral law through reason
Having political freedom from the state
correctAnswer: Giving oneself the moral law through reason
explanation: Autonomy is literally self-legislation: the rational will giving itself the moral law it then obeys. Acting on raw inclination is heteronomy — the agent is moved by forces it did not author. Genuine freedom, for Kant, is the freedom to bind oneself to reason.

prompt: Kant's 'kingdom of ends' is best described as:
options: A theological doctrine of the afterlife
An ideal community of rational agents each treating the others as ends in themselves
A historical state achieved by the French Revolution
A utilitarian aggregate of welfare
correctAnswer: An ideal community of rational agents each treating the others as ends in themselves
explanation: The kingdom (or realm) of ends is the third major formulation of the Categorical Imperative: we should act as legislating members of a community of rational beings, where every agent treats every other as an end in themselves and where the laws of conduct are those that all could rationally endorse.

prompt: Why did Fichte reject Kant's notion of the thing-in-itself?
options: He thought it was empirically refuted
He held that it was an incoherent posit beyond consciousness that nevertheless claimed to affect consciousness
He believed it was a religious doctrine in disguise
He showed it contradicted Newtonian physics
correctAnswer: He held that it was an incoherent posit beyond consciousness that nevertheless claimed to affect consciousness
explanation: Fichte argued that any meaningful talk of the thing-in-itself already places it within consciousness. Worse, Kant's claim that the thing-in-itself 'affects' our sensibility illegitimately applies the category of causality outside experience. Fichte concluded that idealism must drop the thing-in-itself entirely.

prompt: Fichte's first principle is that:
options: Matter is the ultimate reality
The I posits itself, and through that act constitutes both subject and object
The Absolute is unknowable
Sensation is the foundation of all knowledge
correctAnswer: The I posits itself, and through that act constitutes both subject and object
explanation: Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre starts from the absolute self-positing of the I. The I posits itself; it then posits a not-I as its limit; and finally posits both as reciprocally limiting. Reality, in this radicalised idealism, is the self-articulation of rational subjectivity.

prompt: Schelling's Naturphilosophie treats nature as:
options: Inert matter governed only by efficient causes
A self-organising productivity — visible spirit
An illusion of the finite intellect
A mathematical structure devoid of dynamism
correctAnswer: A self-organising productivity — visible spirit
explanation: Worried that Fichte reduced nature to a mere obstacle for the I, Schelling insisted on nature's positive reality. Nature is a hierarchically organised, self-developing productivity; spirit is invisible nature, nature is visible spirit. This influenced Romantic biology and later philosophies of life.

prompt: Hegel's famous jab at Schelling's absolute as 'the night in which all cows are black' was a complaint that:
options: Schelling was insufficiently religious
Schelling's absolute is an empty unity that does not earn its identity through differentiation
Schelling failed to read Kant carefully
Schelling's nature philosophy was unscientific
correctAnswer: Schelling's absolute is an empty unity that does not earn its identity through differentiation
explanation: In the Preface to the Phenomenology, Hegel charged that Schelling's identity-philosophy posited the absolute as the indifference of subject and object without showing how that unity emerges from the labour of distinction. The image: at night every cow looks black — but real knowledge requires articulating differences in daylight.

prompt: The 'positive philosophy' of the late Schelling targeted Hegel for:
options: Insufficient nationalism
Reducing logic to rhetoric
Failing to account for the brute fact of existence as opposed to the structure of essence
Excessive empiricism
correctAnswer: Failing to account for the brute fact of existence as opposed to the structure of essence
explanation: The late Schelling distinguished negative philosophy (the rational analysis of what something is) from positive philosophy (the question of that it is at all). He charged Hegel with mistaking the system of essences for an account of actual existence. Kierkegaard, who attended these Berlin lectures, drew on this critique to launch existentialism.

prompt: The Phenomenology of Spirit shows that the apparently most certain knowledge — 'this, here, now' — actually:
options: Is the foundation of all further knowledge
Cannot be articulated without using universals it claimed to avoid
Should be replaced by mathematics
Is identical to absolute knowing
correctAnswer: Cannot be articulated without using universals it claimed to avoid
explanation: Hegel's analysis of sense-certainty is the opening move. As soon as I try to say what 'this here now' is, I use words like 'this', 'here', 'now' that are universals applicable to any moment or place. The supposedly richest immediate knowledge turns out to be the poorest, forcing consciousness onward to perception.

prompt: In Hegel's master–slave dialectic, what is the eventual outcome?
options: The master attains genuine freedom and recognition
Both parties remain in stable equilibrium
The slave, through labour and self-formation, attains a richer self-consciousness
The struggle leads to mutual destruction
correctAnswer: The slave, through labour and self-formation, attains a richer self-consciousness
explanation: The master can only receive recognition from a being he himself denies as fully human — a hollow recognition. The slave, working on the world and shaping objects in his own image, comes to see himself in his product. The dialectic reverses: it is the bondsman, not the lord, who advances toward authentic self-consciousness.

prompt: What is the key Hegelian thesis that emerges from the master–slave dialectic?
options: Power is the only reality
Self-consciousness is intrinsically social and requires recognition by another self-consciousness
Freedom requires the abolition of all hierarchy
The state is the highest end of human life
correctAnswer: Self-consciousness is intrinsically social and requires recognition by another self-consciousness
explanation: The dialectic dramatises Hegel's structural point: 'self-consciousness exists only in being acknowledged.' I cannot be a self in isolation; selfhood is constituted through mutual recognition with another self I in turn recognise. This makes intersubjectivity foundational, not derivative.

prompt: What does Hegel mean by 'Geist' (Spirit)?
options: A supernatural substance hovering above nature
Individual subjective consciousness
The rational, intersubjective life of a community — its laws, religion, art, science
Pure reason detached from history
correctAnswer: The rational, intersubjective life of a community — its laws, religion, art, science
explanation: Geist is not a ghostly entity. It denotes the historically achieved patterns of mutual recognition — institutions, practices, shared meanings — through which individuals become full selves. Spirit is the 'I that is We and We that is I'.

prompt: Hegel's 'absolute knowing' is best described as:
options: Omniscience about all empirical facts
An exit from history into eternity
Spirit's self-comprehension of its own dialectical journey
The end of philosophy as such
correctAnswer: Spirit's self-comprehension of its own dialectical journey
explanation: Absolute knowing is not an escape from history or a god-like view of every fact. It is the standpoint from which the entire path of consciousness is grasped as a rational unfolding — and that comprehension is itself a moment within spirit, not a leap outside it.

prompt: What does Hegel's term 'Aufhebung' simultaneously mean?
options: To affirm and to ignore
To cancel, preserve, and raise up
To negate and to destroy
To posit and to deny
correctAnswer: To cancel, preserve, and raise up
explanation: Aufheben carries three senses in German that Hegel exploits: to cancel (the position is no longer held in its old form), to preserve (its truth content is retained), and to raise up (it is taken up into a richer category). English usually renders this as 'sublate'. The triple meaning is the heart of the dialectic.

prompt: The 'thesis–antithesis–synthesis' triad commonly attributed to Hegel was actually:
options: Coined by Hegel in the Science of Logic
Originally Marx's contribution
Drawn from Fichte and popularised by later commentators; rarely used by Hegel himself
Invented by Engels
correctAnswer: Drawn from Fichte and popularised by later commentators; rarely used by Hegel himself
explanation: Hegel's actual dialectical movements are diverse — being/nothing/becoming, in-itself/for-itself/in-and-for-itself, etc. The rigid 'thesis–antithesis–synthesis' formula comes mainly from Fichte and was spread by Heinrich Chalybäus's textbook in 1837. Mistaking this for Hegel's method is a common error.

prompt: How does Hegel's Science of Logic begin?
options: With sense-data
With the cogito
With pure being, which proves indistinguishable from pure nothing, their unity being becoming
With axioms borrowed from Euclid
correctAnswer: With pure being, which proves indistinguishable from pure nothing, their unity being becoming
explanation: The Logic opens by attempting to think being with no determinations whatever. Such pure being is empty — exactly like pure nothing. Yet the two are not the same. Their unity-in-difference is becoming. From this minimal start every richer category is supposed to follow by immanent dialectic.

prompt: Hegel summarises world history as:
options: The progress of technological mastery
The progress of the consciousness of freedom
The cyclical return of the same
The decline from a golden age
correctAnswer: The progress of the consciousness of freedom
explanation: For Hegel, in oriental despotisms one was free, in Greek and Roman antiquity some were free, in the modern world all are free in principle. The pattern is not a march toward greater happiness but toward an ever more adequate institutional realisation of the idea that every human being is a free agent.

prompt: The 'cunning of reason' is Hegel's name for:
options: The way philosophers deceive themselves
The way world-historical individuals pursue private aims while serving universal ends they do not understand
The capacity of reason to defeat passion
The unconscious mechanisms of perception
correctAnswer: The way world-historical individuals pursue private aims while serving universal ends they do not understand
explanation: In the Philosophy of History, Hegel observes that figures like Caesar or Napoleon act from particular ambitions yet end up advancing the rational structure of freedom. Reason 'uses' their passions for universal ends. This is the cunning of reason — not a divine plan, but a retrospective intelligibility in history's apparent chaos.
